lead: Standard signals are a small set of functions used as building blocks: the impulse δ(t), step u(t), ramp r(t)=t u(t), and exponential e^(at). Any piecewise signal can be written as a sum of shifted steps, ramps or exponentials. They are also the test inputs for a system, because the response to an impulse or step describes the system completely. In practice they model a switch closing (step), a quantity rising at a steady rate such as constant-velocity motion (ramp), a capacitor discharging (exponential), and a very short hit (impulse).
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for the meaning of t, n, CT and DT; Chapter 1.2 helps for energy and symmetry.

blocks.text: Unit step u(t) is 0 for t<0 and 1 for t≥0. This book uses u(0)=1. In discrete time u[n]=1 for n≥0 and 0 for n<0. The step is a switch: it turns a signal on at t=0. A shifted step u(t−a) turns on at t=a; a negative step −u(t−a) turns off.

blocks.where: x(t) is the signal being sampled; it must be continuous at t=t<sub>0</sub> for this to hold. t<sub>0</sub> is the shifting instant; the integral is over all time.

blocks.text: Unit impulse δ(t) is not an ordinary function. It has δ(t)=0 for t≠0 and unit area ∫ δ(t) dt=1. The value δ(0) is not an ordinary number. Its meaning is the sifting property above: the impulse picks out one value of x.

In discrete time δ[n]=1 at n=0 and 0 elsewhere. It equals u[n]−u[n−1]. The scale rule is δ(at)=δ(t)/|a| for a≠0. The absolute value matters: δ(−2t)=δ(t)/2. Some syllabi call these singularity functions, elementary signals or commonly used signal models.

blocks.where: r(t) is the continuous-time unit ramp; r[n] is the discrete-time unit ramp; u is the unit step.

blocks.text: Unit ramp r(t)=t u(t): r(t)=0 for t<0 and r(t)=t for t≥0. In discrete time r[n]=n u[n]. The ramp is the integral of the step, so r′(t)=u(t). In the generalized sense u′(t)=δ(t). These derivative relations let you differentiate piecewise signals without splitting them into intervals.

blocks.where: e is the base of natural logarithms; j=√−1; ω is angular frequency in rad/s; t is time in s.

blocks.text: Real exponential x(t)=A e<sup>at</sup> u(t) with A and a real. If a<0 the exponential decays; if a>0 it grows; if a=0 it is the constant A. The quantity 1/|a| has units of time and is the time constant for decay. Complex exponential x(t)=e<sup>jωt</sup> has real part a cosine and imaginary part a sine.

In discrete time the complex exponential is e<sup>jΩn</sup>, with Ω in rad/sample; it is periodic only when Ω/(2π) is rational. Complex exponentials are the eigenfunctions of LTI systems, which is why Unit 3 uses them.

Any piecewise signal made of straight segments and jumps can be written with steps and ramps. A jump of height K at t=a is K u(t−a). A pulse of height 2 from t=1 to t=3 is 2u(t−1)−2u(t−3). A slope change at t=a uses a shifted ramp.

Exponentials describe charging, discharging and decay. The product e<sup>at</sup>u(t) means the exponential starts at t=0; before that it is zero. A short pulse can be approximated by an impulse when the system is much slower than the pulse width.

These signals are test inputs. The impulse response h(t) is the output to δ(t); the step response is the output to u(t). They are linked by differentiation and integration. See Unit 2, Continuous-Time LTI Systems, for impulse response and convolution. See Unit 3, Fourier Series and Fourier Transform, for transforms of these signals; see Unit 4, Laplace Transform Analysis, for Laplace transforms.

figure.caption: Unit step, unit ramp, decaying exponential and unit impulse at t=0. The impulse is drawn as a single marker because its height is not an ordinary value; its area is 1.

spec.aria: A plot shows unit step u(t), unit ramp r(t), decaying exponential e^(-t)u(t), and a unit impulse δ(t) at t=0.

examples.question: A voltage signal is x(t)=2u(t+1)−3u(t−2)+4e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t) V. Find x(0), x(3), and dx/dt. Use u(0)=1.
steps: Differentiate each term. d[2u(t+1)]/dt=2δ(t+1). d[−3u(t−2)]/dt=−3δ(t−2). For the exponential term use the product rule: d[e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t)]/dt=−2e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t)+e<sup>−2t</sup>δ(t). Since e<sup>−2t</sup>δ(t)=δ(t), d[4e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t)]/dt=−8e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t)+4δ(t).
examples.check:
import math
x0 = 2.0*1 - 3.0*0 + 4.0*1
x3 = 2.0*1 - 3.0*1 + 4.0*math.exp(-6)
print(x0)
print(round(x3, 3))

traps: δ(t) is not a finite-height pulse. Its value at t=0 is not an ordinary number; use area and sifting only.
This book uses u(0)=1 and u[n]=1 for n≥0. A different convention changes values at the jump but not the area or sifting result.
The scale rule uses |a|: δ(at)=δ(t)/|a|, so δ(−2t)=δ(t)/2, not −δ(t)/2.
When differentiating x(t)u(t), apply the product rule; the δ(t) term comes from the jump at t=0, not from the derivative of x(t).
In DT, δ[n] is 1 only at n=0; it is not a sampled δ(t), and u[n]−u[n−1] gives δ[n].

quiz.a: u(t)=0 for t<0 and 1 for t≥0, with u(0)=1 here. u[n]=1 for n≥0 and 0 for n<0. δ[n]=1 at n=0 and 0 elsewhere.

quiz.q: Why does δ(t) have no ordinary value at t=0?
quiz.a: Its unit area is concentrated at one instant. Only its integral and sifting action are defined; replacing it by a number at t=0 loses the area.

quiz.q: For x(t)=3u(t+2)−2u(t−1) V, find x(0) and x(2).

quiz.a: y′(t)=5δ(t)−15e<sup>−3t</sup>u(t). The δ(t) term comes from the jump at t=0.
δ(2t−4)=δ(2(t−2))=δ(t−2)/2 by the scale rule with |a|=2.

quiz.q: Explain why r′(t)=u(t) and u′(t)=δ(t) in the generalized sense.
quiz.a: The ramp has slope 0 before t=0 and slope 1 after t=0, so its derivative is the step. The step jumps at t=0; the derivative of a jump is a unit-area impulse.

quiz.q: Write a pulse of height 4 from t=1 to t=5 using steps.

beyond: Not for the exam. Impulse and step responses are measured in labs with a pulse generator and oscilloscope; the impulse response of a room is its echo pattern. In control and communications, complex exponentials become phasors and frequency responses. In machine learning, decaying exponentials appear in moving averages and learning-rate schedules. Search terms: singularity functions, impulse response measurement, time constant, Euler's formula, eigenfunction of LTI system.
